Well, I suppose I'm here because things have been getting a bit... tangled up lately. At work, mostly. I'm a jeweler, you see, I do a lot of custom work and repairs, and it's always been a very precise kind of job. You have to be precise with the stones, with the metal, with the customers. I try to answer them, I really do. But instead of just saying "next Friday," my mind sort of... slips the gears. I'll start talking about the repair, and then somehow I'm talking about the invoices I need to file, and from the invoices I start thinking about the garden soil I need to buy because the receipt for the soil was next to the invoice, and before I know it, I'm explaining my mortgage papers to them because the bank called while I was gardening. And I can see it in their faces, doctor. I can see them just completely losing the thread of what I'm saying, looking at me like I'm speaking a different language. It's so frustrating because I know what I want to say, but all these other thoughts just crowd in and spill out all over the counter, so to speak.

It makes me look so unprofessional.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, yes, I do get this... this awful physical feeling when the thoughts start piling up like that. It's like a buzzing, and I actually... I start doing this thing with my hands. When I get anxious about losing my train of thought and looking foolish in front of a customer, I'll rub my fingers together. And I don't just mean a little nervous fidget, I mean I will rub them together so hard and for so long that they actually get completely raw and sore. As a jeweler, your fingertips are everything, you know? You absolutely need that tactile sensitivity to feel if a bezel is perfectly smooth or if a tiny prong is catching on a polishing cloth, but I just rub and rub my fingers together like I'm trying to buff a deep scratch out of a piece of brass. I don't even realize I'm doing it until it hurts.

And the strangest part is, while I have all that nervous, tense energy making me wear out my own skin, the rest of me feels... heavy. My husband actually pointed it out just the other evening. He was sitting in the back room while I was trying to finish up a ring sizing, and he says I move so much slower at the bench now. He told me it looked like I was moving underwater. Even just reaching out and picking up my tweezers—the fine-point titanium ones I use for placing little melee diamonds, the ones with the really delicate tips—it just feels like it takes so much physical effort. It's like my arms weigh a hundred pounds each. 

So I've got this frantic, anxious rubbing going on with my fingers, but actually trying to do a deliberate physical task at the bench? It's just incredibly slow and exhausting. I used to fly through those repairs, my hands just dancing over the bench pin, but now every little movement feels like such a chore. It’s so frustrating because my mind is racing with all these jumbled thoughts, but my body is just dragging.

And I can see it in their faces, doctor. I can see them just completely losing the thread of what I'm saying, looking at me like I'm speaking a different language. It's so frustrating because I know what I want to say, but all these other thoughts just crowd in and spill out all over the counter, so to speak.\n\nDoctor: Are these difficulties with staying on topic and following conversations affecting your relationships with your customers or impacting your work performance?\n\nPatient: Oh, yes, it really is. It’s... it's taking a terrible toll, honestly, and it breaks my heart because I've built this business from the ground up. I’ve actually had to cut way back on my custom work, which used to be my absolute favorite part of the job. There's nothing quite like sitting down with someone and sketching out a completely unique design, you know? But lately, during those client consultations, I just... I completely lose track of what we're doing. A bride will be talking about the specific bezel setting she wants for her grandmother's diamond, and I'll try to explain the process, but then I'm rambling about the history of platinum alloys, and by the end of the hour, I haven't even taken down her ring size or given her a quote. \n\nAnd because everything gets so jumbled up in my head, I'm missing my repair deadlines left and right. I used to be so incredibly punctual. If I told a customer their chain would be soldered by Tuesday, it was polished and in a little velvet pouch by Monday afternoon. Now, the days just sort of bleed together, and suddenly it's Thursday and the necklace is still sitting in the safe, untouched, and the customer is standing right there in the shop looking at me. It makes me look so unprofessional. \n\nEven the paperwork... well, the paperwork is a whole other disaster. I used to handle all the invoices myself. I prided myself on keeping the books immaculate, making sure every supplier was paid for every ounce of silver wire or polishing compound. But now, I'll look at an invoice and the numbers and line items just sort of swirl into other thoughts. I've had to ask my husband to start double-checking all of them for me. He has to come into the shop after he finishes his own workday, bless him, and he sits at the little desk in the back room just to make sure I haven't overpaid a vendor or completely forgotten to bill a customer for a sizing job. I never used to need help like that. I've been doing this for decades, and now I can't even get through a basic invoice without him having to fix my mistakes.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself forgetting things that you would normally remember, such as appointments or tasks?\n\nPatient: Well, no, actually, it's not my memory at all. That’s the strange part, you see. I actually have a wonderful memory, I always have. If I have an appointment, say, a dentist appointment on a Thursday at 2:15, I know it's at 2:15. I don't need a reminder call or anything like that. And with the shop, I know exactly what needs to be done. I remember that the clasp on Mrs. Peterson's pearl necklace needs to be replaced with a 14-karat gold lobster clasp, not a spring ring, because spring rings catch on her scarves—she wears those lovely silk scarves, you know the ones, hand-painted, usually from Italy, she told me her daughter brings them back for her every summer. \n\nSo the task itself, the memory of it, is perfectly intact in my brain. I don't forget that the necklace is sitting there in the safe. It's just that when I go to actually sit at the jeweler's bench and do the task, or when I try to explain the repair to her, that's when all those other thoughts just rush in and take over. I haven't forgotten to order the polishing compound or the silver flux, I just... I get lost in my own head on the way to doing it, if that makes sense. \n\nBut the actual remembering? No, I don't have any trouble with that. My memory is sharp as a tack, honestly. I can still tell you the exact inventory numbers for the sterling silver box chains we carried back in 1998, which is completely useless information now, of course, since that supplier went out of business years ago, but it's still right there in my head. So, no, I really wouldn't say I'm forgetting things. It's more of a traffic jam of thoughts rather than a blank space, if you know what I mean.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your difficulties with staying on topic and following conversations are affecting your personal relationships outside of work?\n\nPatient: Well, I haven't really noticed it causing a problem at home, honestly. My husband, bless him, he's just... he's so patient. We've been married for twenty-eight years this coming October—we got married right in the middle of autumn because I always loved the colors of the leaves changing, you know, those deep russet reds and the bright golds. It always reminded me of the different shades of citrine and garnet when you hold them up to the light. Anyway, he knows me so well by now. When we're sitting at the dinner table, and I start talking about a new supplier for rhodium plating, and then somehow end up talking about the neighbor's dog digging up my hydrangeas, and then suddenly I'm wondering out loud if we need to get the chimney swept before winter... he just sits there and nods. He doesn't look at me like I'm crazy or like I've lost my mind, the way the customers do. I don't even realize I'm doing it until it hurts.\n\nAnd the strangest part is, while I have all that nervous, tense energy making me wear out my own skin, the rest of me feels... heavy. It's like my arms weigh a hundred pounds each. \n\nSo I've got this frantic, anxious rubbing going on with my fingers, but actually trying to do a deliberate physical task at the bench? It's just incredibly slow and exhausting. I used to fly through those repairs, my hands just dancing over the bench pin, but now every little movement feels like such a chore. I mean, it's more that I worry they think I'm just terribly unprofessional or maybe that I don't care about their pieces. And that's what really breaks my heart, because I care so much. When someone brings in their grandmother's engagement ring, or a locket that's been in the family for four generations, they are trusting me with their history, you know? It's not just metal and stones, it's memories. Like this one lady, Mrs. Higgins, she brought in a cameo brooch last month—beautiful carved shell, probably late Victorian, with this delicate seed pearl halo—and she wanted it converted into a pendant because she doesn't wear brooches. 

And I knew exactly how to do it, I could see the whole process in my head, how I'd solder a hidden bail onto the back without damaging the shell, which is so tricky because heat can just ruin those old cameos in a second if you aren't careful. But when I tried to explain the process to her, to reassure her that her heirloom was safe with me, my thoughts just started tumbling over each other. I started talking about the melting point of silver solder, and then somehow I was talking about the different types of torches, and then I think I mentioned something about the price of propane going up... and I could see her face just sort of freeze. She looked at me like I was a completely different person than the jeweler she'd been coming to for ten years. 

She didn't say anything mean, she just sort of gathered up her purse and said she needed to think about it, and she took the cameo and left. And I just stood there, feeling so foolish. I didn't think she thought I was crazy, but I knew she thought I wasn't capable anymore. And that's... that's almost worse, isn't it? To have people look at you and decide they can't trust you to do the one thing you've dedicated your whole life to doing. So, no, I don't sit around worrying that people think I belong in an asylum or anything dramatic like that. But I do see the confusion in their eyes, and the hesitation, and it just makes me want to sink right through the floorboards. It's just so embarrassing to not be able to articulate what I know is right there in my head.

Oh, the guilt... it’s just awful. It doesn't just stop when the customer leaves the shop, you know. I take it all home with me. I'll go home and I just replay it all in my head, over and over again. Every single awkward conversation, like the one with Mrs. Higgins, or when I stammered through explaining a simple prong retipping to Mr. Abernathy last week... I just lie awake in bed, staring at the ceiling—we have that textured popcorn ceiling, the kind they put in during the late seventies, and I keep meaning to have it scraped but who has the time or the money right now—and I just replay every stutter, every confused look, and every single repair that I’ve had to delay because I’m moving so slowly at the bench. 

I just replay all of it like it's this undeniable proof that I’m a burden. And that's when the guilt really, really sets in, because I think about the shop and the financial side of things. A few years ago, we took out a second mortgage on the house to expand the storefront. We wanted to put in these beautiful new cherry wood display cases with built-in LED lighting, because the old halogen lights were just so hot and they made all the white gold and platinum look a bit yellow, which you absolutely don't want. It was a big risk, but we thought it was an investment. 

But now... now I keep thinking I’ve completely ruined our future by taking on that mortgage. If I can't even talk to the customers without scaring them off, and if I can't finish the repairs on time because my hands feel like lead, how on earth are we going to pay for it? My husband is so patient, like I told you, he really is a saint. He works so hard at his own job—he's in logistics, coordinating freight shipments, which is stressful enough with all the supply chain issues they've been having lately—and then he comes home to me, just sitting there uselessly, rubbing my fingers raw and crying over a late ring sizing. It's just suffocating. Every time I mess up a conversation or fall behind on a piece, it just feels like more proof that I'm dragging him down, and that I've doomed us both with that mortgage all because I wanted a prettier shop that I can't even run properly anymore.

Well, I suppose the thoughts are just as jumbled when I'm by myself, honestly. I’ll be sitting completely alone at my workbench—it’s this beautiful old maple jeweler's bench that I bought second-hand when I first started out, it has all these wonderful little shallow drawers for my burs and my needle files—and my mind will still be racing, or sometimes it just goes completely blank. But as for how I actually behave... I didn't even realize how much had changed until my husband pointed it out to me. 

You see, when I'm alone, I think I'm just working normally, maybe just feeling a bit tired. But he comes into the shop sometimes to bring me lunch, usually just a turkey sandwich from the little deli next door because he knows I forget to eat, and he says I'm just... I'm physically different. He says I move so much slower at the bench now. It's like I'm moving underwater. He was watching me try to prep a setting for a small sapphire the other day, and he told me later that it looked like even picking up my tweezers was taking this monumental effort. And these are my favorite tweezers! They're fine-tipped titanium, they weigh absolutely nothing, they're specifically designed to be an extension of your hand so you don't get hand fatigue when you're sorting tiny melee diamonds for pave work. But he's right, lately they feel like they weigh ten pounds. My arms just feel like lead when I'm sitting there by myself.

But then, on the flip side, when I'm around people or when I get really overwhelmed and anxious about a customer interaction, I do this entirely different thing. I don't even realize I'm doing it half the time until it physically hurts, but I'll just sit there and rub my fingers together. I'll rub the pads of my thumbs against my index and middle fingers, just over and over and over again, almost frantically, until the skin is completely raw and sore. Which is terrible, because as a jeweler, your hands are your entire livelihood. You need your calluses to handle the hot metal, but you also need absolute sensitivity to feel the tension when you're pushing a prong over a delicate stone. But I just rub them and rub them until they ache. So I guess... whether I'm alone and moving like molasses, or feeling anxious and rubbing my hands raw, my body just isn't acting the way it's supposed to anymore.

I'll start talking about the repair, and then somehow I'm talking about the invoices I need to file, and from the invoices I start thinking about the garden soil I need to buy because the receipt for the soil was next to the invoice, and before I know it, I'm explaining my mortgage papers to them because the bank called while I was gardening. And I can see it in their faces, doctor. I can see them just completely losing the thread of what I'm saying, looking at me like I'm speaking a different language. It's so frustrating because I know what I want to say, but all these other thoughts just crowd in and spill out all over the counter, so to speak.\n\nDoctor: Are these difficulties with staying on topic and following conversations affecting your relationships with your customers or impacting your work performance?\n\nPatient: Oh, yes, it really is. I completely lose track of what we're doing. A bride will be talking about the specific bezel setting she wants for her grandmother's diamond, and I'll try to explain the process, but then I'm rambling about the history of platinum alloys, and by the end of the hour, I haven't even taken down her ring size or given her a quote. \n\nAnd because everything gets so jumbled up in my head, I'm missing my repair deadlines left and right. I've been doing this for decades, and now I can't even get through a basic invoice without him having to fix my mistakes.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself forgetting things that you would normally remember, such as appointments or tasks?\n\nPatient: Well, no, actually, it's not my memory at all. I haven't forgotten to order the polishing compound or the silver flux, I just... I get lost in my own head on the way to doing it, if that makes sense. \n\nBut the actual remembering? No, I don't have any trouble with that. My memory is sharp as a tack, honestly. When we're sitting at the dinner table, and I start talking about a new supplier for rhodium plating, and then somehow end up talking about the neighbor's dog digging up my hydrangeas, and then suddenly I'm wondering out loud if we need to get the chimney swept before winter... he just sits there and nods. Well... I suppose... yes. It’s strange, I haven't really wanted to admit this to anyone, not even my husband, because he already has enough on his plate with the freight logistics and all, but... yes. Sometimes, especially when the shop is completely quiet, like in the late afternoons when the foot traffic just completely dies down on our street... I'll be sitting out front at my bench, and I'll hear a woman's voice. Just a low mutter, but she's definitely saying my name. And it always sounds like it's coming from the polishing room in the back. 

We have the polishing room separated by this heavy fireproof door because of the dust collection system—you know, polishing compounds like rouge and Tripoli create this incredibly fine particulate dust, and you absolutely have to have a good ventilation hood or you'll be breathing it in all day, which is just terrible for your lungs over the years. So it's a separate room entirely. But I'll hear this woman muttering my name from back there, clear as day. 

And then... there's also a smell. Sometimes I'll just be sitting there, trying to focus on a piece, and suddenly I get this incredibly strong whiff of burning metal. Now, as a jeweler, you know exactly what that smells like. It's usually the smell of the flux burning off when you're soldering, or if you accidentally get the torch too close to a piece of steel binding wire and it sparks. It has this very distinct, sharp, acrid smell that catches right in the back of your throat. But the thing is, I'll smell it when my torches are completely off. The main oxygen and propane tanks will be entirely valved off at the wall—I'm always so paranoid about gas leaks, so I make absolutely sure to bleed the lines and shut the main valves the second I'm done soldering for the day—but I'll still smell that sharp, burning scent just filling the room. 

And it feels so incredibly real. Both the voice and the smell, they're so vivid that I actually get up from my bench, put down my tools, and walk all the way to the back of the shop to check. I'll push open the polishing room door expecting to see a customer who somehow wandered back there by mistake, or I'll go check all the torch connections again, just sniffing the air around the hoses. But there's never anyone there, and the tanks are always cold and shut tight. I just end up standing there in the empty shop, looking for someone who isn't there and a fire that doesn't exist. It's just so unnerving.

No, I wouldn't say it's tied to any one specific thought or... or a particular worry playing on a loop in my head, if that's what you mean. It's not like I'm sitting there thinking, "Oh dear, did I leave the pickle pot plugged in?"—which is a terrible thing to do, by the way, because if the acid solution boils dry it creates this toxic fume and absolutely ruins the copper tongs. Or I'm not obsessing over whether I miscalculated the alloy ratios for a custom rose gold pour. It’s nothing concrete like that. 

It’s really more just... this overwhelming wave of general anxiety that washes over me, usually when there's just too much external pressure all at once. Like, if a customer comes in wanting to redesign an entire heirloom estate collection. That actually happens more often than you'd think. People inherit these gorgeous Art Deco platinum rings, but they want the European-cut diamonds pulled out and the platinum melted down into something modern, which always breaks my heart just a little bit because the hand-pierced filigree work from the 1920s is just nearly impossible to replicate today with modern wax casting methods. But anyway, when someone is standing there at the counter, expecting me to be bubbly and creative and attentive, and maybe the shop phone is ringing at the same time, and I'm just feeling that heavy, awful sadness I mentioned... I just start rubbing my fingers. 

It's completely unconscious. I'm not trying to fix a bad thought in my head by doing it, or trying to prevent something bad from happening. My body just sort of takes over and does it on its own because the general pressure of existing in that moment is just too much. I'll just rub and rub the pads of my fingers together while I'm nodding at the customer, and I truly don't even realize I'm doing it until the friction actually burns the top layer of skin off. So, no, no specific thoughts... just my body's way of short-circuiting when everything gets to be too much, I suppose.

I prided myself on keeping the books immaculate, making sure every supplier was paid for every ounce of silver wire or polishing compound. But now, I'll look at an invoice and the numbers and line items just sort of swirl into other thoughts. I've had to ask my husband to start double-checking all of them for me. He has to come into the shop after he finishes his own workday, bless him, and he sits at the little desk in the back room just to make sure I haven't overpaid a vendor or completely forgotten to bill a customer for a sizing job. I never used to need help like that. I've been doing this for decades, and now I can't even get through a basic invoice without him having to fix my mistakes.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself forgetting things that you would normally remember, such as appointments or tasks?\n\nPatient: Well, no, actually, it's not my memory at all. That’s the strange part, you see. I actually have a wonderful memory, I always have. If I have an appointment, say, a dentist appointment on a Thursday at 2:15, I know it's at 2:15. I don't need a reminder call or anything like that. And with the shop, I know exactly what needs to be done. It's more of a traffic jam of thoughts rather than a blank space, if you know what I mean.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your difficulties with staying on topic and following conversations are affecting your personal relationships outside of work?\n\nPatient: Well, I haven't really noticed it causing a problem at home, honestly. It’s so frustrating because my mind is racing with all these jumbled thoughts, but my body is just dragging.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever worry that people might think you're losing your mind or that there's something seriously wrong with you when you have trouble staying on topic or explaining things?\n\nPatient: Well, I don't... I wouldn't say I worry that they think I'm losing my mind, exactly. Not in those words. I mean, it's more that I worry they think I'm just terribly unprofessional or maybe that I don't care about their pieces. And that's what really breaks my heart, because I care so much. When someone brings in their grandmother's engagement ring, or a locket that's been in the family for four generations, they are trusting me with their history, you know? It's not just metal and stones, it's memories. I started talking about the melting point of silver solder, and then somehow I was talking about the different types of torches, and then I think I mentioned something about the price of propane going up... and I could see her face just sort of freeze. She looked at me like I was a completely different person than the jeweler she'd been coming to for ten years. \n\nShe didn't say anything mean, she just sort of gathered up her purse and said she needed to think about it, and she took the cameo and left. I just lie awake in bed, staring at the ceiling—we have that textured popcorn ceiling, the kind they put in during the late seventies, and I keep meaning to have it scraped but who has the time or the money right now—and I just replay every stutter, every confused look, and every single repair that I’ve had to delay because I’m moving so slowly at the bench. \n\nI just replay all of it like it's this undeniable proof that I’m a burden. Like this one lady, Mrs. Higgins, she brought in a cameo brooch last month—beautiful carved shell, probably late Victorian, with this delicate seed pearl halo—and she wanted it converted into a pendant because she doesn't wear brooches. \n\nAnd I knew exactly how to do it, I could see the whole process in my head, how I'd solder a hidden bail onto the back without damaging the shell, which is so tricky because heat can just ruin those old cameos in a second if you aren't careful. But when I tried to explain the process to her, to reassure her that her heirloom was safe with me, my thoughts just started tumbling over each other. I started talking about the melting point of silver solder, and then somehow I was talking about the different types of torches, and then I think I mentioned something about the price of propane going up... and I could see her face just sort of freeze. She looked at me like I was a completely different person than the jeweler she'd been coming to for ten years. \n\nShe didn't say anything mean, she just sort of gathered up her purse and said she needed to think about it, and she took the cameo and left. And I just stood there, feeling so foolish. I didn't think she thought I was crazy, but I knew she thought I wasn't capable anymore. And that's... that's almost worse, isn't it? To have people look at you and decide they can't trust you to do the one thing you've dedicated your whole life to doing. So, no, I don't sit around worrying that people think I belong in an asylum or anything dramatic like that. But I do see the confusion in their eyes, and the hesitation, and it just makes me want to sink right through the floorboards. It's just so embarrassing to not be able to articulate what I know is right there in my head.\n\nDoctor: Do you often feel guilty or ashamed after you've had trouble explaining something to a customer or keeping your thoughts organized?\n\nPatient: Oh, the guilt... it’s just awful. It doesn't just stop when the customer leaves the shop, you know. I take it all home with me. I'll go home and I just replay it all in my head, over and over again. Every single awkward conversation, like the one with Mrs. Higgins, or when I stammered through explaining a simple prong retipping to Mr. Abernathy last week... I just lie awake in bed, staring at the ceiling—we have that textured popcorn ceiling, the kind they put in during the late seventies, and I keep meaning to have it scraped but who has the time or the money right now—and I just replay every stutter, every confused look, and every single repair that I’ve had to delay because I’m moving so slowly at the bench. \n\nI just replay all of it like it's this undeniable proof that I’m a burden. And that's when the guilt really, really sets in, because I think about the shop and the financial side of things. A few years ago, we took out a second mortgage on the house to expand the storefront. We wanted to put in these beautiful new cherry wood display cases with built-in LED lighting, because the old halogen lights were just so hot and they made all the white gold and platinum look a bit yellow, which you absolutely don't want. It was a big risk, but we thought it was an investment. \n\nBut now... now I keep thinking I’ve completely ruined our future by taking on that mortgage. If I can't even talk to the customers without scaring them off, and if I can't finish the repairs on time because my hands feel like lead, how on earth are we going to pay for it? My husband is so patient, like I told you, he really is a saint. He works so hard at his own job—he's in logistics, coordinating freight shipments, which is stressful enough with all the supply chain issues they've been having lately—and then he comes home to me, just sitting there uselessly, rubbing my fingers raw and crying over a late ring sizing. It's just suffocating. Every time I mess up a conversation or fall behind on a piece, it just feels like more proof that I'm dragging him down, and that I've doomed us both with that mortgage all because I wanted a prettier shop that I can't even run properly anymore.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel a significant difference in your mood when you're not at work or dealing with customers?\n\nPatient: I wish I could say yes. I really wish I could tell you that as soon as I lock the front door of the shop and turn the 'Closed' sign around, all of this just lifts off me. But... no, it doesn't work like that at all. Honestly, it starts before I even leave the house. Most mornings I wake up with this... this flat, heavy sadness. It's like the color has completely drained out of the house before I even get to the shop. \n\nI'll just be sitting there at the kitchen island—we put in this lovely absolute black granite a few years ago, and it's usually so beautiful when the morning sun hits the little flecks of mica in the stone—but lately, I just sit there with my coffee, and everything just feels so gray and lifeless. It doesn't matter if I have a completely free Sunday with no customers to worry about, or if I'm just sitting in my own living room in my slippers. That heavy, flat feeling is just... it's already there the second I open my eyes. \n\nI used to love my mornings, you know? Waking up early, listening to the birds, maybe sketching out a new custom pendant design while the house was quiet and my husband was still asleep. I had this special sketchbook just for my morning ideas. But now, I just stare at the countertop and feel this awful weight. It doesn't matter where I am or who I'm talking to, the sadness is just sitting right there on my chest. So, getting away from work doesn't really change it at all. The environment changes, sure, but that gray feeling just follows me everywhere I go.\n\nDoctor: Do you notice any difference in how your thoughts are organized or how you behave when you're by yourself compared to when you're with other people?\n\nPatient: Well, I suppose the thoughts are just as jumbled when I'm by myself, honestly. I’ll be sitting completely alone at my workbench—it’s this beautiful old maple jeweler's bench that I bought second-hand when I first started out, it has all these wonderful little shallow drawers for my burs and my needle files—and my mind will still be racing, or sometimes it just goes completely blank. But he comes into the shop sometimes to bring me lunch, usually just a turkey sandwich from the little deli next door because he knows I forget to eat, and he says I'm just... I'm physically different. He says I move so much slower at the bench now. It's like I'm moving underwater. It has this very distinct, sharp, acrid smell that catches right in the back of your throat. But the thing is, I'll smell it when my torches are completely off. I just start rubbing my fingers. \n\nIt's completely unconscious. I'm not trying to fix a bad thought in my head by doing it, or trying to prevent something bad from happening. My body just sort of takes over and does it on its own because the general pressure of existing in that moment is just too much. Well, yes and no, I suppose. It’s... it's not like my hands have a mind of their own, exactly. I mean, I *could* stop if I really focused on it, maybe? Gosh, a habit or something I must do... I really don't know how to answer that, to be perfectly honest with you. I'm not sure it neatly fits into either of those boxes. 

When I think of a habit, I think of things I do at the bench without thinking, but that actually serve some sort of purpose, you know? Like, over the years, I've developed this habit of always tapping my tweezers on the edge of the soldering block before I pick up a piece of gold, just to make sure there's no stray flux or old solder stuck to the tips. That's a habit. I don't have to do it, but I've just done it for so long that it's second nature. Or how I always wipe down my bench pin with a leather chamois before I start filing, just to keep the silver dust from getting cross-contaminated. 

But the finger rubbing... it doesn't feel like that. It's not a habit I developed over time like tapping my tweezers. But at the same time, I wouldn't say it's something I absolutely feel I must do, either. It's not like this driving urge where my brain is screaming at me that I have to rub my fingers together right that very second. 

It is more like... well, I don't know. I really don't. It just sort of starts happening on its own. I'll just be sitting there, maybe trying to focus on setting a tiny little two-millimeter sapphire into a bezel, which takes an incredible amount of concentration, by the way, because if you push the bezel rocker even a fraction of a millimeter too hard, you can chip the stone. Sapphires are hard, sure, but they can still cleave if you hit them at the wrong angle with a steel tool. And while I'm trying to focus through all this heavy, awful sadness, I'll suddenly realize my other hand is just rubbing and rubbing in my lap. My fingers get so rough anyway from the needle files and the emery paper that I can practically hear the skin catching when I do it. 

So I don't know if that makes it a habit or a necessity or what. I've never really stopped to think about the exact definition of it. I wish I could give you a better answer, a simple one or the other, but I honestly just don't know how to label it. It's just something my hands do when everything else feels like too much.

Well, you ask about outside of work, but honestly, when you own a small independent jewelry store and your husband is your main help... there really isn't much of a boundary between personal life and work life. So, yes, it’s affecting everything. Everything just feels like it's slipping through my fingers, and he's the only one trying to catch it all.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, outside of the shop... yes. Though, I suppose even my hobbies are still somewhat tied to jewelry, but they were strictly for me, you know? Just for fun, not for the business or for paying customers. But even those... I just don't do them anymore. 

I used to absolutely love hunting for old clasps. Oh, I could spend an entire Sunday morning just scouring estate sales, antique fairs, those dusty little flea markets out in the county. There is just something so incredibly special about vintage findings. You can find these exquisite, hand-pierced filigree box clasps from the 1920s, or these really heavy, solid brass spring rings that they simply do not manufacture anymore because the tooling costs would be too high today. I would dig through absolute junk boxes, getting my hands completely filthy, just to find one or two salvageable clasps that I could clean up and use for a personal project, maybe stringing some old glass beads I'd found. It was like a treasure hunt. 

And on top of that, I used to spend my evenings planning these little jewelry classes. Just very informal, low-pressure gatherings. Sometimes I'd do it for the community center, or just invite a few ladies from the neighborhood over. I would spend hours putting together these neat little kits with copper wire and some inexpensive semi-precious chips, and I'd teach them basic wire-wrapping techniques, or how to properly turn a loop for a French hook earring. It was so much fun, and it was so rewarding to see someone's face light up when they realized they had actually made a wearable piece of jewelry with their own two hands. I had all these little compartmentalized trays that I would organize the class materials into, sorting everything by size and color...

But lately... I just can't bring myself to do any of it. I haven't been to a single estate sale in months. And the classes? The very thought of trying to organize one just makes me feel exhausted. Sometimes, my husband will actually bring my hobby trays out to the living room after dinner, I think hoping that seeing my vintage stash will spark something in me, cheer me up a bit. But I just... I mostly stare at the trays. I look at all those little compartments filled with beautiful old toggle clasps and vintage glass, and I just feel this heavy, awful emptiness. I look at them and I just feel like none of it is worth starting. What's the point? I'll look at a clasp that just needs a quick polish with a sunshine cloth, and instead of feeling inspired, it just feels like climbing a mountain. So I just sit there staring at the little compartments until I finally just ask him to put the lids back on and put them away in the closet. It breaks my heart a little, because that was my escape, you know? But the joy is just completely gone from it.

I prided myself on keeping the books immaculate, making sure every supplier was paid for every ounce of silver wire or polishing compound. But now, I'll look at an invoice and the numbers and line items just sort of swirl into other thoughts. I've had to ask my husband to start double-checking all of them for me. He has to come into the shop after he finishes his own workday, bless him, and he sits at the little desk in the back room just to make sure I haven't overpaid a vendor or completely forgotten to bill a customer for a sizing job. I never used to need help like that. I've been doing this for decades, and now I can't even get through a basic invoice without him having to fix my mistakes.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself forgetting things that you would normally remember, such as appointments or tasks?\n\nPatient: Well, no, actually, it's not my memory at all. I don't need a reminder call or anything like that. And with the shop, I know exactly what needs to be done. I haven't forgotten to order the polishing compound or the silver flux, I just... I get lost in my own head on the way to doing it, if that makes sense. \n\nBut the actual remembering? No, I don't have any trouble with that. My memory is sharp as a tack, honestly. It's more of a traffic jam of thoughts rather than a blank space, if you know what I mean.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your difficulties with staying on topic and following conversations are affecting your personal relationships outside of work?\n\nPatient: Well, I haven't really noticed it causing a problem at home, honestly. It always reminded me of the different shades of citrine and garnet when you hold them up to the light. Anyway, he knows me so well by now. I used to love my book club. We were reading historical fiction mostly, though last year we did a whole series on biographies of famous women, which was fascinating. At home, it's just... well, it's just me being me, and my husband is used to that, thank goodness. I'm not trying to ward off any bad luck or prevent a disaster. Honestly, most of the time, I'm just trying to survive the next five minutes of a conversation without bursting into tears right there over the glass display cases. So, no, there's no conscious thought of preventing anything bad. It just happens.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you have no control over the action of rubbing your fingers together when it happens?\n\nPatient: Well, yes and no, I suppose.
